lessons.title: How the Crude Oil Market Works: Brent, WTI, OPEC+ and India's Import Bill

children.text: When a drone strike hits an oil facility in the Gulf, the effects reach an Indian investor within hours. Brent crude jumps, the rupee weakens, shares of paint companies and airlines fall, shares of ONGC rise, and MCX crude oil opens sharply higher in the evening session. No other commodity is tied so directly to India's economy and markets. By the end of this lesson you will know how the global crude market is organised, the difference between Brent, WTI and Dubai, how OPEC+ and US shale shape supply, and why every $10 move in oil matters to India's import bill, the rupee, inflation and the Nifty.

body.text: India imports most of the oil it uses, so crude oil is effectively a tax or a tax cut on the entire Indian economy. Higher oil means a bigger import bill, pressure on the rupee, higher inflation risk and squeezed margins for oil-consuming companies.

children.text: Not All Crude Is the Same
Crude oil varies by how dense it is and how much sulphur it contains, and those qualities decide how easy it is to refine into petrol and diesel.

markDefs.definition: A measure of how heavy or light a crude oil is compared with water. Higher API gravity means lighter crude, which usually yields more petrol and diesel.

children.text: Light vs heavy.
Density is measured by
API gravity
. Lighter crude has a higher API gravity and yields more high-value fuels. Heavier crude needs more complex refining.
Sweet vs sour.
Crude with low sulphur content is called sweet; crude with high sulphur content is sour. Sweet crude is easier and cheaper to refine.

markDefs.definition: Reference grades of crude oil, such as Brent, WTI and Dubai, whose prices are used to price thousands of other physical cargoes at a premium or discount.

children.text: Because quality varies, the world prices oil off a few
benchmark crudes
, and other grades trade at a premium or discount to them.

body.label: The Indian basket
body.value: A mix of sour Dubai and Oman grades with sweet Brent
body.context: The Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) publishes the price of the Indian crude basket, a weighted average reflecting the sour and sweet crude Indian refiners actually process. Sour grades make up the larger share.

body.title: Name the crude
body.textWithBlank: Crude oil with a low sulphur content, which is easier to refine, is described as ___ crude.
body.explanation: Low-sulphur crude is sweet and high-sulphur crude is sour. Brent and WTI are both light, sweet crudes, while Dubai and Oman are medium, sour grades.

children.text: Who Supplies the World's Oil
The world uses more than 100 million barrels of oil a day. Three groups shape how much is supplied.

markDefs.definition: The alliance of OPEC members, led by Saudi Arabia, and non-OPEC producers, led by Russia, that has coordinated oil production targets since late 2016.

children.text: OPEC+.
OPEC was founded in 1960, and since late 2016 it has coordinated output with non-OPEC producers led by Russia as
OPEC+

. By raising or cutting production targets, the group tries to steer prices. Its most dramatic move came in April 2020, when it agreed a record cut of about 9.7 million barrels a day as COVID crushed demand.
US shale.

The United States is now the world's largest crude producer. Shale wells can be drilled and brought online within months, so US output responds to prices faster than big conventional projects, and acts as a check on how high OPEC+ can push prices for long.
Everyone else.
Producers such as Canada, Brazil, Norway and Guyana add supply through large projects that take years to develop.

markDefs.definition: Oil production capacity that is not being used but can be brought online quickly, held mainly by Saudi Arabia and a few other OPEC+ members. Low spare capacity makes prices more vulnerable to supply shocks.

children.text: The key concept is
spare capacity
: how much extra oil producers could pump quickly if needed. When spare capacity is high, supply shocks are absorbed. When it is low, even a small disruption can send prices soaring.

body.title: What oil traders watch every week

children.text: US inventory data: the weekly US Energy Information Administration report, released on Wednesdays, showing whether crude stocks rose or fell.
OPEC+ meetings: decisions on production targets, and whether members actually comply.
Geopolitics: tensions affecting the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, Russia and other key supply routes.
Demand signals: Chinese import data, global manufacturing surveys and travel activity.
The dollar: oil is priced in dollars, so a stronger dollar can weigh on prices.

body.text: Oil's swings come from the same inelasticity you learned about in Chapter 1, at global scale. Drivers cannot stop commuting and airlines cannot stop flying just because fuel costs more, and new supply takes months or years. So small imbalances between supply and demand produce very large price moves.

children.text: 1. The Import Bill and the Rupee
India pays for imported crude in dollars. When oil prices rise, oil companies need more dollars, which puts pressure on the rupee and widens the current account deficit.

body.latex: \text{Change in annual import bill} \approx \Delta\text{Price per barrel} \times \text{Barrels imported per day} \times 365
body.caption: A simple approximation that ignores changes in volumes, discounts and refined product exports.

body.title: A $10 oil shock
body.prompt: Assume India imports 4.7 million barrels of crude a day. If the average crude price rises by $10 a barrel for a full year, by roughly how many billion US dollars does the annual crude import bill rise? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: $10 × 4.7 million barrels × 365 days = $17,155 million, or about $17.2 billion. That extra demand for dollars is one reason the rupee tends to weaken when oil spikes.

children.text: 2. Inflation and Government Finances

Crude feeds into petrol, diesel, cooking gas, transport costs and thousands of products made from petrochemicals. A sustained oil spike can push up CPI inflation and complicate RBI's rate decisions. The government also carries part of the burden through subsidies, such as on LPG, and through choices on excise duty.

body.title: Show me the math: what a barrel costs per litre

children.text: Say Brent is $80 a barrel and USD/INR is 84 (illustrative).
Price per barrel in rupees: $80 × 84 = ₹6,720
Price per litre of crude: ₹6,720 ÷ 159 litres = about ₹42.26

Compare that with petrol at around ₹95 a litre in Delhi in 2024 and 2025. The raw crude is well under half of the pump price. The rest is refining, freight, marketing, dealer commission, and central excise duty plus state VAT. That is also why retail petrol prices in India have often stayed unchanged for long periods even while global crude moved a lot.

body.title: Crude cost per litre
body.prompt: Brent is $75 a barrel and USD/INR is 86. What is the cost of crude per litre in rupees, rounded to two decimal places? Use 159 litres per barrel.

children.text: 3. Winners and Losers in the Stock Market

body.caption: How higher crude prices tend to affect Indian listed sectors

cells: They sell crude, so realisations rise, unless the government imposes windfall taxes
Input costs rise faster than they can pass on at the pump
Depends on refining margins, not just the crude price
Many raw materials are crude derivatives
Aviation turbine fuel is one of the biggest costs
Synthetic rubber and carbon black are crude-linked

body.text: Windfall taxes show how policy changes the equation. In July 2022, after crude spiked, the government imposed a special additional excise duty on domestic crude production, capping how much of the price rise producers like ONGC could keep. It was scrapped in December 2024.

body.title: Who gains from a spike?
body.question: Brent rises 20% over a month on supply disruptions, and the government does not change taxes. Which company is most likely to see a direct positive impact on earnings?
body.explanation: ONGC produces and sells crude oil, so higher prices raise its realisations. Airlines, paint makers and tyre makers all use crude-linked inputs, so their costs rise.

body.title: Oil spikes overnight
body.scenario: Aarti, a 35-year-old IT professional in Noida, wakes up to news that tensions in the Middle East have escalated and Brent is up 8% overnight. She holds a diversified equity mutual fund, some shares of Asian Paints and IndiGo, a gold ETF, and she is thinking of buying MCX crude oil futures in the evening session to "catch the rally".
body.prompt: How might each part of her portfolio be affected, and what should she think about before buying crude futures?
body.modelAnswer:
Likely effects:
1. Diversified equity fund: markets often fall on oil shocks because of inflation, rupee and margin worries, though oil producers inside the fund may gain.
2. Asian Paints and IndiGo: both are crude consumers, so their shares often fall on sharp oil spikes.
3. Gold ETF: geopolitical fear and a weaker rupee can support the rupee price of gold, partly offsetting losses elsewhere.
4. The rupee itself may weaken, which also lifts MCX crude prices in rupee terms.

Before buying crude futures:
1. An 8% overnight gap means she would be buying after the move. Geopolitical spikes can reverse fast if supply is not actually disrupted.
2. Crude is highly volatile, and a single Crude Oil lot covers 100 barrels. She should size the trade on a realistic adverse move, perhaps using Crude Oil Mini.
3. Buying crude could also be thought of as a hedge for her crude-sensitive stocks, but only if sized to match that exposure, not as a leveraged bet.
4. She should know the contract expiry and that MCX crude is cash settled against the NYMEX WTI price.

points: Crude is priced off benchmarks: Brent globally, WTI in the US and for MCX, and Dubai and Oman for Middle Eastern crude sold to Asia.
Quality matters: light, sweet crude is easier to refine than heavy, sour crude.
OPEC+ steers supply through production targets, while fast-responding US shale acts as a check.
Low spare capacity and inelastic demand make oil prices swing violently, as 2008, 2020 and 2022 showed.
India imports more than 85% of its crude, so every $10 move affects the import bill by billions of dollars, the rupee and inflation.
Higher crude tends to help upstream producers like ONGC and hurt consumers like paints, airlines and tyres.
